summary: A republication of PKCS #10 version 1.7 from RSA Laboratories, defining a syntax for certification requests. Change control remains within the PKCS process.

plainLanguage.summary: To get an official digital ID, you fill in a form with your name and your public key and sign it with your private key. This document defines that form, so any office that issues certificates can read it.

subtitle: The standard form for asking a certificate authority to turn your public key into a certificate.

tldr.problem: An entity that holds a key pair needs a standard way to ask a certification authority for an X.509 certificate that binds its name to its public key.
tldr.mechanism: A certification request holds a distinguished name, a public key and optional attributes, signed with the subject's own private key. It is defined in ASN.1 and DER encoded before signing.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2986 republishes PKCS #10 version 1.7 from RSA Laboratories and leaves change control with the PKCS process. It obsoletes RFC 2314 and is updated by RFC 5967.

today: RFC 2986 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 2314 and is updated by RFC 5967. It says change control stays with the PKCS process.

sections.title: What a Certification Request Is
sections.content:
A certification request consists of a distinguished name, a public key and optionally a set of attributes, all signed by the entity requesting certification. It is sent to a certification authority, which transforms it into an X.509 public-key certificate. How the authority returns the new certificate is outside the scope of the document; a PKCS #7 message is named as one possibility.

The attributes serve two purposes: to give other information about the entity, such as a challenge password it may later use to request revocation, and to supply attributes for inclusion in X.509 certificates. A non-exhaustive list of attributes appears in PKCS #9. Authorities may also require non-electronic forms and return non-electronic replies, and the preliminary intended application is to support PKCS #7 cryptographic messages.

The RFC states that it is a republication of PKCS #10 v1.7, that change control stays with the PKCS process, and that its body, apart from the security considerations section, is taken directly from the PKCS #9 v2.0 or PKCS #10 v1.7 documents.
sections.plainLanguage: You write down your name and your public key, sign the page with your private key, and hand it to the office that issues digital ID cards.

sections.title: How a Request Is Built and Used
sections.content:
A request has three parts: the certification request information, a signature algorithm identifier, and a digital signature over the information. The requester first builds a CertificationRequestInfo value holding a subject distinguished name, a subject public key and optionally a set of attributes. It signs that value with the subject's private key, then collects the value, the algorithm identifier and the signature into a CertificationRequest.

The certification authority fulfils the request by authenticating the requesting entity and verifying its signature. If the request is valid it constructs an X.509 certificate from the distinguished name and public key, the issuer name, and its own choice of serial number, validity period and signature algorithm. If the request carries PKCS #9 attributes, the authority may also use them to build certificate extensions.

The RFC adds notes: an entity would typically send a request after generating a key pair, but may also do so after a change of name. The signature stops an entity from requesting a certificate for another party's public key. How the request reaches the authority is out of scope, and both paper and electronic forms are possible. The syntax is not compatible with the Privacy-Enhanced Mail request syntax of RFC 1424, because it allows attributes, omits the issuer name, serial number and validity period, and does not require an innocuous message to be signed.
sections.plainLanguage: The office checks who you are and checks that the signature really is yours. It then prints the certificate with its own serial number and expiry date, and it may copy extra details from the form into the certificate.

sections.title: The Request Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax is written in ASN.1. CertificationRequestInfo is a SEQUENCE of four things: version, subject, subjectPKInfo and attributes. The version shall be 0 for this version of the standard. The subject is the distinguished name of the entity whose public key is to be certified. subjectPKInfo is a SubjectPublicKeyInfo value: an AlgorithmIdentifier naming the key algorithm and its parameters, plus a bit string holding the public key. Examples of public-key algorithms include the rsaEncryption object identifier from PKCS #1. The attributes are a set of optional extra information.

CertificationRequest is a SEQUENCE of the certificationRequestInfo value, a signatureAlgorithm (AlgorithmIdentifier) and a signature bit string. The algorithm objects and attribute objects are limited by information object sets, and definitions of specific ones are left to specifications that reference this document. Those specifications stay interoperable with future versions if new objects are added after the extension marker.

The ASN.1 module is given in an appendix under the object identifier iso(1) member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549) pkcs(1) pkcs-10(10) modules(1) pkcs-10(1).
sections.plainLanguage: The form has fixed boxes in a fixed order: a version number, your name, your public key, any extra details, and at the end the method you used to sign and the signature itself.

sections.title: Signing the Request
sections.content:
Signing takes two steps. First the certificationRequestInfo value is DER encoded, giving an octet string. Second, that octet string is signed with the certification request subject's private key under the specified signature algorithm, giving the bit string stored in signature.

For the signature algorithm, the RFC gives PKCS #1's md5WithRSAEncryption as an example of an ALGORITHM object that a specification might add to the information object set SignatureAlgorithms. It also shows an equivalent way to write the top-level type using a generic SIGNED wrapper that contains the value to be signed, the algorithm and the signature.
sections.plainLanguage: You turn the completed form into a fixed string of bytes, then stamp it with your private key. Anyone can check the stamp against your public key, so nobody else could have produced it.

sections.title: Version 1.7 and Security
sections.content:
Version 1.7 refers to X.680 through X.690, the then-current international standards for ASN.1 and its encoding rules, and removes all references to X.208 and X.209. It notes that X.690 requires encoded SET OF components to be sorted in ascending order under DER, but applications should not rely on the ordering of attribute components. All references to PKCS #6 Extended-Certificate Syntax were removed because RSA Laboratories was withdrawing support for it after extensions were added to X.509 version 3 certificates. The number 1.7 was chosen to avoid confusion with RFC 2314, which is named version 1.5, and an unsupported version 1.6.

The security considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are discussed throughout the memo. The RFC was published as an Informational memo, with change control retained in the PKCS process.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition tidies the old form, points to the current rule books for writing data, and drops a feature that was being retired.
